analysis.one_liner: Charges royalties on all natural gas lost to venting, flaring, or leaks from federal drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill says that companies drilling for gas on federal land and offshore waters must pay the government royalties on all the gas they produce — including gas that is vented, burned off, or accidentally leaked, not just gas that gets sold. It keeps a 2024 rule that cracked down on gas waste in force and blocks a 2026 proposal to replace it with a weaker version unless the replacement provably reduces waste or improves air quality.
analysis.who_benefits: The public gains twice: the federal government collects royalties on gas that companies currently burn off or let escape for free, and less methane — a potent greenhouse gas — goes into the air near drilling sites. People living near federal leases get cleaner air, and taxpayers get paid for a resource that currently evaporates without compensation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near gas wells

how_it_helps.text: For new federal leases, royalties must be assessed on all gas produced, including gas consumed or lost by venting, flaring, or negligent equipment releases, with narrow exceptions for emergencies under 48 hours, gas used on-site, and unavoidably lost gas.

The bill requires the Bureau of Land Management to enforce its April 2024 rule on waste prevention and royalties, and blocks it from finalizing a June 2026 proposed replacement rule unless the replacement is certified to further cut gas waste or improve air quality and public health.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land and offshore waters pay more: gas they currently vent, flare, or lose through negligent leaks would become royalty-owing rather than free. Companies with substantial federal lease holdings would bear the cost, and some of it could be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Higher royalties on lost gas raise production costs, and producers may pass some of that on to energy consumers through higher prices.

The royalty requirement applies only to leases issued after enactment, so existing leases would continue under current rules for years, limiting how much revenue or pollution reduction the bill produces near-term.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a straightforward waste problem: gas produced from public land currently escapes without royalty payment, costing taxpayers revenue and adding methane to the air. The cost falls on producers who lose gas, and the emergency and on-site-use exceptions narrow the scope sensibly. The main honest limitation is that it only reaches new leases, so its benefits build slowly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee in August 2026, and the committee has not acted on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Luz Rivas introduced the Methane Pollution Accountability Act on August 6, 2026, with Reps. Huffman and Norton as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and the action history shows no hearings, markup, or floor action since.
Three House Democrats are listed as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers on federal land are better off so far: with the bill stalled in committee, no royalties are charged on vented, flared, or negligently lost gas, and the path to finalizing a weaker 2026 replacement rule remains open.

for.name: Rep. Luz Rivas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring royalties on all gas produced from federal land and offshore leases.

for.name: Reps. Jared Huffman and Eleanor Holmes Norton

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats are recorded supporting the bill — a sponsor and three cosponsors, all Democrats — and no member is recorded opposing it, since it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal land and offshore leases
industries.note: The bill makes gas the companies vent, flare, or negligently lose royalty-owing instead of free, and locks in the stricter 2024 waste-prevention rule while blocking a proposed 2026 replacement. Their savings from the current system come at the expense of federal royalties and cleaner air.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Natural Resources Committee with three cosponsors and no committee action. In a House where Republicans hold 223 of 441 seats and the bill has no recorded Republican support, the most likely path is that it stays in committee until the Congress ends without a hearing or vote.
